extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, legal scholars, USPTO examiners, and software developers concerned with US patent eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether computer-implemented inventions are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the Supreme Court's Alice/Mayo two-part framework and related USPTO and court guidance. Focus is on distinguishing abstract ideas from patent-eligible applications and identifying what counts as an 'inventive concept' or 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-part test (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-step framework: (1) whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept; and (2) if so, whether the claim contains an inventive concept sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principal eligibility filter applied post-Alice. The Court incorporated the Mayo analysis and used it to assess computer-implemented inventions. Apply step one to identify judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas); if present, proceed to step two to look for an 'inventive concept' that is 'significantly more' than the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to-abstract-idea inquiry (step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is 'drawn to' an abstract idea (a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the Court treated as abstract include 'intermediated settlement' and other fundamental economic practices 'long prevalent in our system of commerce.' If the claim's focus is the abstract idea itself rather than a particular application, it fails step 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-concept / 'significantly more' (step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application—i.e., whether it provides 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court held that merely 'appending conventional steps, specified at high level of generality' is insufficient. The inventive concept must do more than implement the abstract idea on a generic computer; it must improve a technological process or otherwise add meaningful limitations that prevent pre-emption of the underlying idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-emption rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether granting the patent would 'monopolize' basic tools of innovation and thereby pre-empt future use of the underlying idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusionary principle is framed as preventing pre-emption: patents should not disproportionately tie up the use of fundamental building blocks. If a claim effectively grants a monopoly over an abstract idea, it weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely mandate a generic computer to perform generic computer functions do not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court expressly rejected the idea that implementing an abstract idea on a computer automatically qualifies for §101 protection. Look for claim limitations that go beyond conventional computer functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: System claims substantively treated like method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling a claim as a 'system' or reciting 'specific hardware' does not by itself make a claim patent-eligible if its substance is the same as an abstract method claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court cautioned against interpreting §101 to depend on the 'draftsman's art.' Examiners and courts will examine the substance over form; drafting as system vs. method cannot be used to evade the Alice test.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO examples of judicial exceptions (non-exhaustive list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO provided illustrative subject-matter examples that fall within judicial exceptions to §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative items include: an isolated DNA; a correlation that is the consequence of how a certain compound is metabolized in the body; electromagnetism to transmit signals; creating a contractual relationship; using advertisement as an exchange or currency; processing information through a clearinghouse; managing a game of bingo. These examples help identify abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that can qualify as 'significantly more' (examples from USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claim limitations may transform a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter by supplying 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO lists examples (not exclusive) of qualifying limitations: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with, or by the use of, a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing. Claims exhibiting these features are more likely to survive §101 scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely appending conventional steps is an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Appending conventional or well-understood routine steps at a high level of generality will not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that adding routine computer functions or generic steps, without more, does not convert an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention. Examiners and courts will disregard conventional activities framed at high generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be examined under other patentability requirements as well
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 analysis does not replace examination for novelty, nonobviousness, written description, enablement, and other requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO instructed that all claims are to be fully examined under each of the other patentability requirements. §101 is an additional filter, not a substitute for other substantive examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show 'substantially more' and rejection of 'creative writing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Software developers and applicants bear the burden of showing their claims provide 'substantially more' than an abstract idea; creative drafting alone is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article concludes that the two-part Alice test has 'narrowed the scope' of software patent protection and places the burden on applicants to demonstrate that claims supply substantially more than abstract ideas rather than relying on creative claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts will look to substantive essence over 'patent-ese' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will be 'careful to avoid allowing the typically convoluted claim language—"patent-ese"—to obfuscate the general purpose and real essence of software patent claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating eligibility, focus on the real substance and purpose of the claimed invention rather than being misled by complex or jargon-heavy claim drafting. Claims that disguise an abstract idea with convoluted language remain at risk under Alice.
